xix-a: Overview of Alternative Investments
Which feature most clearly distinguishes alternative investments such as private equity from traditional listed equity?
Daily exchange-traded pricing
Guaranteed minimum returns
Lower minimum ticket sizes than mutual funds
Lower liquidity and less frequent, less transparent pricing
Private assets are not traded on an exchange, so they are illiquid and valued only periodically, unlike listed shares.
Overview of Alternative Investments
An HNI says she wants to add private equity mainly because it is 'uncorrelated with everything'. What is the most accurate response?
Private equity has zero correlation with listed markets by regulation
Private equity always moves opposite to listed equity
Private assets can diversify a portfolio, but reported low correlation is partly due to infrequent, appraisal-based valuations
Correlation is irrelevant for illiquid assets
Smoothed, periodic valuations understate measured volatility and correlation, so the diversification benefit is real but overstated by reported numbers.
Overview of Alternative Investments
Which of the following is generally treated as an alternative asset class?
Listed large-cap shares
Government treasury bills
Bank fixed deposits
Venture capital
Venture capital invests in unlisted early-stage companies and falls outside traditional stocks, bonds and cash.
Alternative Investment Funds in India
Under the SEBI (AIF) Regulations, 2012, an AIF is best described as a privately pooled investment vehicle that:
Collects funds from investors for investing according to a defined investment policy for their benefit
Accepts deposits from the public and pays fixed interest
Is a scheme of a SEBI-registered mutual fund
Is a portfolio of individually held securities managed for one client
The AIF definition centres on a privately pooled vehicle investing under a stated policy; mutual funds and PMS are covered by separate regulations.
Alternative Investment Funds in India
A fund that provides risk capital to early-stage start-ups would ordinarily register under which AIF category?
Category I
Category II
Category III
It cannot register as an AIF
Venture capital funds, including angel funds, are a sub-category of Category I AIFs, which invest in sectors seen as socially or economically desirable.
Alternative Investment Funds in India
A private equity fund investing in growth-stage unlisted companies, with no special incentives and no leverage, would typically be registered as:
Category I AIF
Category II AIF
Category III AIF
A mutual fund scheme
Category II is the residual category for funds such as PE and debt funds that are neither Category I nor Category III and do not use leverage.
Alternative Investment Funds in India
Special situation funds, which invest in stressed assets, are classified under:
Category II AIF
Category III AIF
Real estate investment trusts
Category I AIF
SEBI introduced special situation funds as a sub-category of Category I AIFs to invest in stressed loans and assets.
Concepts in the AIF Industry
In a typical AIF, the 'commitment' of an investor refers to:
The amount paid upfront on signing
The total amount the investor agrees to contribute over the fund's life, drawn down as needed
The fund manager's personal investment
The NAV of the investor's units on a given date
Investors commit capital upfront but pay it in tranches through drawdowns (capital calls) as the manager finds investments.
Concepts in the AIF Industry
An investor committed ₹2 crore to a Category II AIF. The manager has so far called 40% of commitments. How much commitment remains uncalled?
₹80 lakh
₹1.2 crore
₹2 crore
₹1.6 crore
Called = 40% × ₹2 crore = ₹80 lakh; uncalled = ₹2 crore − ₹80 lakh = ₹1.2 crore.
Concepts in the AIF Industry
The 'J-curve' in private equity describes:
A steady linear rise in NAV from inception
The shape of a fund's fee schedule
Negative early returns due to fees and costs, followed by gains as investments mature and are exited
Rising leverage over the fund life
Fees and set-up costs hit early while value creation and exits come later, so cumulative returns dip before rising.
Concepts in the AIF Industry
The 'hurdle rate' in an AIF fee structure is:
The maximum management fee the manager may charge
The rate at which uncalled capital earns interest
The minimum return investors must earn before the manager is entitled to carried interest
The penalty rate for a defaulting investor
Carry is shared only after investors receive their preferred return, i.e. the hurdle.
Concepts in the AIF Industry
A fund earns ₹50 crore profit on ₹100 crore of contributed capital. Carried interest is 20% with no hurdle. What is the manager's carry?
₹20 crore
₹5 crore
₹8 crore
₹10 crore
Carry = 20% × ₹50 crore profit = ₹10 crore.
AIF Regulatory Framework
The minimum corpus required for each scheme of an AIF is:
₹5 crore
₹50 crore
₹20 crore
₹100 crore
The AIF Regulations require each scheme (other than angel funds, which have separate rules) to have a corpus of at least ₹20 crore.
AIF Regulatory Framework
Ignoring accredited investors and employees/directors of the manager, the minimum investment an individual must make in an AIF is:
₹10 lakh
₹25 lakh
₹50 lakh
₹1 crore
The general minimum ticket is ₹1 crore; a lower ₹25 lakh limit applies to employees or directors of the AIF/manager, and accredited investors are exempt.
AIF Regulatory Framework
A Category II AIF has a corpus of ₹300 crore. What is the minimum continuing interest the sponsor or manager must hold?
₹7.5 crore
₹10 crore
₹5 crore
₹15 crore
For Category I and II it is the lower of 2.5% of corpus (₹7.5 crore) and ₹5 crore, i.e. ₹5 crore.
AIF Regulatory Framework
Apart from angel funds, the maximum number of investors permitted in a single AIF scheme is:
No limit
The AIF Regulations cap each scheme (other than angel funds) at 1,000 investors.
AIF Regulatory Framework
Can a Category II AIF borrow money to make investments?
No, it may borrow only temporarily to meet day-to-day operational needs, within SEBI limits
Yes, up to two times its NAV
Yes, without any limit if investors agree
Only by issuing listed bonds
Category I and II AIFs cannot use leverage for investment; only short-term borrowing for operational needs is permitted.
AIF Regulatory Framework
The tenure of a close-ended Category I or II AIF may be extended beyond its stated life:
By up to two years, with approval of two-thirds of unit holders by value
Indefinitely at the manager's discretion
Only with prior approval of the RBI
By up to five years with a simple majority of investors by number
The regulations allow a maximum two-year extension subject to approval of two-thirds of investors by value of their investment.
Alternative Investment Fund Structuring
In India, most AIFs are set up as:
Public limited companies
Trusts
Partnership firms under the 1932 Act
Co-operative societies
The trust structure is preferred for flexibility, ease of distribution and tax pass-through for Category I and II.
Alternative Investment Fund Structuring
In a trust-structured AIF, the document that governs the investor's commitment and drawdown obligations is the:
Contribution agreement
Memorandum of association
Certificate of incorporation
Scheme information document
The contribution agreement between investor, trustee and manager records commitment, drawdowns, fees and other rights.
Alternative Investment Fund Structuring
Which party in a trust-based AIF holds the fund's assets on behalf of the beneficiaries?
The distributor
The investment committee
The trustee
The placement agent
The trustee holds the trust property for the beneficiaries and oversees the manager under the trust deed.
Alternative Investment Fund Structuring
A foreign investor wants exposure to an Indian Category II AIF. A common structure for pooling several offshore investors is:
Registering the AIF as a mutual fund
An offshore feeder vehicle that invests into the Indian AIF
Investing through a PMS account in the AIF manager's name
Converting the AIF into a company
Offshore feeders aggregate foreign investors and invest into the onshore AIF, simplifying KYC and tax treatment for those investors.
Risk and Return – Fund and Investor Perspective
For a Category I or II AIF, the most appropriate return measure that captures the timing of capital calls and distributions is:
Simple average annual return
Time-weighted daily NAV return
Dividend yield
Internal rate of return (IRR)
Because the manager controls the timing of cash flows, money-weighted IRR is the standard measure for closed-ended private funds.
Risk and Return – Fund and Investor Perspective
A fund has paid-in capital of ₹100 crore, has distributed ₹80 crore and holds a residual NAV of ₹70 crore. What is its TVPI?
TVPI = (Distributions + Residual value) / Paid-in = (80 + 70) / 100 = 1.5x.
Risk and Return – Fund and Investor Perspective
Using the same fund (paid-in ₹100 crore, distributions ₹80 crore, NAV ₹70 crore), the DPI is:
DPI = Distributions / Paid-in = 80 / 100 = 0.8x; it counts only cash actually returned.
Risk and Return – Fund and Investor Perspective
Which risk is most specific to an investor in a close-ended private equity AIF?
Liquidity risk, because capital is locked in until the fund exits investments
Daily NAV volatility risk
Interest rate reset risk on deposits
Counterparty risk on exchange-traded futures
Investors generally cannot redeem before maturity, so the inability to access capital is the key risk.
Investment Process and Governance of Funds
In an AIF, the investment committee's principal role is to:
Market the fund to new investors
Approve investment and exit decisions in line with the fund's strategy and PPM
Act as custodian of the fund's securities
Calculate tax payable by each investor
The investment committee scrutinises and approves deals; its members are responsible for decisions taken within the PPM framework.
Investment Process and Governance of Funds
A Category II AIF wishes to invest in a company that is an associate of its sponsor. What is required?
Only the trustee's consent
Approval of at least 75% of investors by value of their investment
Prior approval of the stock exchange
Nothing, since the deal is at market price
Investments in associates are a conflict of interest and need approval of 75% of investors by value.
Investment Process and Governance of Funds
Under the AIF Regulations, a Category I or II AIF may invest in a single investee company up to:
10% of its investable funds
25% of its investable funds
50% of its investable funds
100% if disclosed in the PPM
Category I and II AIFs face a 25% single-company concentration limit (large value funds for accredited investors have a higher limit).
Investment Process and Governance of Funds
A Category II AIF has investable funds of ₹400 crore. Applying the general concentration limit, the most it can put into one investee company is:
₹100 crore
₹40 crore
₹200 crore
₹80 crore
25% × ₹400 crore = ₹100 crore.
Fund Due Diligence – Investor Perspective
When doing due diligence on a first-time fund manager, an investor should place the greatest weight on:
The fund's brochure design
The team's attributable track record, stability and alignment of interest
Projected IRRs in the pitch deck alone
The number of distributors selling the fund
Without a fund-level history, the team's past deals, cohesion and skin in the game are the best evidence of capability.
Fund Due Diligence – Investor Perspective
Operational due diligence on an AIF primarily examines:
Only the macroeconomic outlook
Back-office processes, valuation policy, custody, compliance and controls
The investor's own risk appetite
The stock exchange listing of the fund
Operational DD tests whether non-investment processes are robust enough to protect investor assets and reporting.
Fund Due Diligence – Investor Perspective
Which of the following is a red flag in AIF due diligence?
A clearly documented valuation policy
Use of a reputed independent custodian
A sponsor commitment above the regulatory minimum
Frequent unexplained turnover of key investment professionals
Key-person churn threatens execution of the strategy and often signals internal problems.
Fund Due Diligence – Investor Perspective
An investor compares two PE funds with the same IRR. Fund X achieved it with mostly realised exits; Fund Y largely through unrealised marks. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
Fund X's performance is more reliable because it is backed by cash returned
Fund Y is superior because unrealised gains are untaxed
Both are identical in quality
Fund Y is safer because it has not sold assets
Realised returns (high DPI) are certain, whereas unrealised marks depend on valuation assumptions.
Legal Documentation and Negotiation – Investor Perspective
The Private Placement Memorandum (PPM) of an AIF is mainly meant to:
Serve as the trust's registration certificate
Act as a contract note for each drawdown
Replace KYC documents
Disclose the fund's strategy, risks, fees, terms and the manager's background to prospective investors
The PPM is the primary offer document giving investors the information needed to make an informed decision.
Legal Documentation and Negotiation – Investor Perspective
A 'key person' clause in an AIF agreement typically provides that:
The key person receives all carried interest
Investors must stay invested even if all key staff leave
The distributor is the key person
If named key professionals leave, the investment period may be suspended until investors approve a replacement
It protects investors who committed capital on the strength of specific individuals.
Legal Documentation and Negotiation – Investor Perspective
A large investor negotiates a side letter granting it any better terms later offered to others. This right is called:
Clawback
Drag-along right
Catch-up
Most favoured nation (MFN) clause
An MFN clause entitles the investor to terms as favourable as those given to comparable investors.
Legal Documentation and Negotiation – Investor Perspective
A 'clawback' provision in AIF documents protects investors by:
Allowing the fund to recall distributions to pay management fees
Letting investors withdraw at any time
Requiring the manager to return carried interest that turns out to be excess on final reckoning
Capping the fund's total expenses
If early deals pay carry but later losses mean total carry was overpaid, the manager must give back the excess.
Fund Monitoring, Reporting and Exit
During the life of a close-ended AIF, which of the following is a common exit route for the fund's portfolio investments?
Initial public offering or strategic sale of the investee company
Redemption of units by the investee company
Daily repurchase by the AIF
Conversion into bank deposits
PE funds realise value by taking companies public, selling to strategic buyers or other funds, or by buybacks.
Fund Monitoring, Reporting and Exit
If an AIF makes a material change to its PPM, dissenting investors must ordinarily be:
Offered an option to exit the scheme
Forced to accept the change
Charged a penalty for objecting
Shifted to a mutual fund scheme
SEBI requires that investors who do not agree to material changes be given an exit option.
Fund Monitoring, Reporting and Exit
When a close-ended AIF reaches the end of its tenure with some investments still unsold, one outcome allowed under SEBI's framework is:
Automatic conversion into an open-ended fund
Write-off of the investments to zero
Distribution of the unsold investments to investors in specie, subject to investor approval
Transfer of the investments to the distributor
SEBI's liquidation framework permits in-specie distribution or a liquidation scheme for unliquidated investments with investor consent.
Valuation
Valuation of unlisted investments held by Category I and II AIFs is required to be carried out by:
The distributor who sold the fund
The investee company's own management only
An independent valuer, following a disclosed valuation methodology
Any investor holding the most units
Independence avoids conflicts, since manager fees and reported performance depend on valuations.
Valuation
For a young start-up with no revenue that recently raised money from an arm's-length investor, the most suitable starting point for valuation is often:
Dividend discount model
The price of the recent investment round, adjusted for subsequent developments
Book value of fixed assets
Liquidation value
With no earnings or cash flows to model, a recent arm's-length price is a key reference, calibrated for later changes.
Valuation
Which valuation approach values a mature, profitable unlisted company by applying peer multiples like EV/EBITDA?
Market (comparable companies) approach
Cost approach
Net asset approach
Replacement value approach
Applying listed peer or transaction multiples to the company's metrics is the market approach.
Taxation – India Specific
For Category I and II AIFs, income other than business income is generally taxed:
Only at the fund level at the maximum marginal rate
Neither in the fund's nor the investors' hands
In the hands of investors, as if they had invested directly (pass-through)
Only when the fund is wound up
Indian tax law gives Category I and II AIFs pass-through status for non-business income.
Taxation – India Specific
If a Category II AIF earns business income, that income is:
Exempt in the fund's hands and taxed in the investor's hands
Taxed at the fund level, not passed through
Fully exempt
Taxed only for foreign investors
Pass-through is denied for business income, which is taxed at the AIF level.
Taxation – India Specific
The pass-through regime for Category I and II AIFs means an investor needs to know:
Only the total amount distributed
Only the fund's NAV
The nature of the income (capital gains, interest, dividend) allocated to them, as reported by the fund
Nothing, since all income is exempt
Because tax is levied as if the investor earned the income directly, its character determines the investor's tax treatment.
Good Practices
An AIF distributor is approached by a retired client with ₹1.2 crore of total savings who needs regular income. Recommending that she commit ₹1 crore to a 10-year PE fund is:
Suitable, because she meets the minimum ticket size
Suitable, because PE returns are higher
Unsuitable, because it concentrates her savings in an illiquid product that does not match her income need
Acceptable if she signs a risk disclaimer
Meeting the minimum investment does not make a product suitable; liquidity needs and concentration matter.
Good Practices
Under SEBI's direct plan requirement for AIFs, a direct plan:
Is available only to foreign investors
Charges a higher management fee
Is allowed only for Category III
Carries no distribution fee or placement fee
Investors approaching an AIF directly or through a SEBI-registered investment adviser can invest via a direct plan without distribution charges.
Good Practices
For Category I and II AIFs (other than certain exempt cases), distribution commission must be paid:
Entirely upfront at first close
Largely on an equal trail basis, with at most one-third of the total distribution fee payable upfront
Only on exit of the fund
As a percentage of the carried interest
SEBI moved AIF commissions toward trail payments to reduce mis-selling, permitting only a limited upfront portion for Category I and II.
xix-b: Overview of Alternative Investments
Hedge-fund-style strategies are usually described as 'absolute return' strategies because they:
Aim to generate positive returns across market conditions rather than merely beat an index
Guarantee a fixed return every year
Track an index with zero tracking error
Invest only in government securities
Absolute return funds target returns independent of market direction, using tools such as shorting and hedging.
Overview of Alternative Investments
Compared with a long-only equity mutual fund, a typical hedge fund strategy is more likely to:
Be restricted to large-cap stocks
Offer daily liquidity with no lock-in
Use short selling, derivatives and leverage
Be sold to retail investors with ₹500 SIPs
Hedge strategies rely on flexible tools like shorting, derivatives and leverage that mutual funds use only in limited ways.
Overview of Alternative Investments
Which statement about the risk of alternative investments is correct?
Alternatives always have lower risk than equities
Alternative assets cannot lose capital
Risk in alternatives is measured only by credit rating
Reported volatility may understate true risk when assets are illiquid or infrequently priced
Smoothed pricing of illiquid holdings can make returns look less volatile than economic reality.
Overview of Alternative Investments
An investor allocates 10% of his portfolio to a market-neutral strategy. The most likely objective is to:
Maximise exposure to an equity rally
Earn a fixed coupon
Add returns with low correlation to the direction of the equity market
Eliminate all risk from the portfolio
Market-neutral funds balance long and short exposure to reduce market beta, so returns come mostly from stock selection.
Growth of AIFs in India and Suitability of Category III AIFs
Which feature makes Category III AIFs different from Category I and II AIFs?
They must invest only in unlisted start-ups
They receive tax pass-through status
They may employ leverage and complex trading strategies, including derivatives
They cannot invest in listed securities
Category III funds trade with a view to short-term returns and may use leverage, unlike Category I and II.
Growth of AIFs in India and Suitability of Category III AIFs
Category III AIFs, unlike Category I and II AIFs, may be structured as:
Only close-ended
Only interval schemes
Only exchange-traded funds
Open-ended or close-ended
Category I and II AIFs must be close-ended, while Category III may be either.
Growth of AIFs in India and Suitability of Category III AIFs
Which investor is generally most suitable for a leveraged long-short Category III AIF?
A first-time investor seeking capital protection
A retiree depending on the investment for monthly expenses
An investor who needs the money within three months
A financially sophisticated investor with a high risk appetite and investable surplus well beyond the minimum ticket
Leverage and complex strategies suit investors who understand them and can absorb losses without affecting their essential needs.
Growth of AIFs in India and Suitability of Category III AIFs
A client has a total financial portfolio of ₹1.5 crore. Placing ₹1 crore of it in a single Category III fund is a concern mainly because of:
Exceeding the maximum investment limit
The fund being unable to accept individuals
Concentration risk relative to the client's overall wealth
Tax being levied twice
Two-thirds of wealth in one complex strategy concentrates risk, even though the ₹1 crore minimum is met.
Growth of AIFs in India and Suitability of Category III AIFs
A Category III AIF that mainly invests in listed equities with a long-only, concentrated approach would compete most directly with:
Bank recurring deposits
Portfolio management services and active equity mutual funds
Venture capital funds
Infrastructure investment trusts
Long-only Category III funds offer listed equity exposure similar to PMS and active mutual funds, differing in structure, fees and taxation.
Introduction to Category III AIF Ecosystem
In a Category III AIF, the entity that sets up the fund and contributes the continuing interest is the:
Sponsor
Custodian
Registrar and transfer agent
Auditor
The sponsor establishes the AIF and must maintain the required continuing interest in the scheme.
Introduction to Category III AIF Ecosystem
Which entity is responsible for investment decisions and day-to-day management of a Category III AIF?
The trustee
The distributor
The investment manager
The valuer
The manager runs the portfolio within the PPM; the trustee oversees, and others provide services.
Introduction to Category III AIF Ecosystem
A prime broker typically provides a Category III AIF with:
Distribution of fund units to retail investors
Statutory audit of accounts
Securities lending, financing, trade clearing and custody-related services
Registration of the fund with SEBI
Prime brokers support hedge-fund strategies with leverage, stock borrowing and consolidated clearing.
Introduction to Category III AIF Ecosystem
An AIF distributor's role in the Category III ecosystem is primarily to:
Decide which stocks the fund buys
Value the portfolio at month-end
Hold investors' units in safe custody
Identify suitable investors, explain the product and its risks, and facilitate onboarding
Distributors are responsible for sales conduct and suitability, not investment or operational functions.
Category III AIF: Fund Structures and Service Providers
Most Category III AIFs in India are set up as trusts. The trustee's role is to:
Execute the fund's trades
Market the fund
Oversee that the fund is managed in line with the trust deed and investors' interests
Compute investors' tax returns
The trustee holds trust property and supervises the manager's compliance with the trust deed and PPM.
Category III AIF: Fund Structures and Service Providers
Why must a Category III AIF appoint a custodian?
To guarantee investor returns
To safekeep the fund's securities independently of the manager
To approve investment decisions
To act as the fund's distributor
Independent custody reduces the risk of misuse of assets; SEBI requires AIFs to appoint a custodian.
Category III AIF: Fund Structures and Service Providers
The fund accountant or fund administrator of a Category III AIF is mainly responsible for:
Sourcing new investors
Choosing the fund's benchmark index
Approving investment committee decisions
Maintaining books of accounts and computing NAV
Fund administration covers accounting, NAV computation and investor records.
Category III AIF: Fund Structures and Service Providers
A Category III fund running a long-short strategy needs to borrow shares to short. This service is usually arranged through:
The fund's statutory auditor
Securities lending and borrowing via a prime broker or exchange mechanism
The registrar and transfer agent
The trustee's bank account
Short sales require borrowing shares, typically through SLB facilities arranged via brokers.
Category III AIF: Fund Structures and Service Providers
Units issued by AIFs to investors are now required to be held in:
Physical certificates only
Dematerialised form
Bearer form
Unregistered form at the manager's office
SEBI requires AIF units to be dematerialised, improving transparency and record-keeping.
Regulatory Framework
For Category III AIFs, SEBI caps leverage such that gross exposure does not exceed:
One time the NAV
Five times the NAV
Two times the fund's NAV
Ten times the NAV
Category III AIFs may use leverage only up to a gross exposure of 2x NAV.
Regulatory Framework
A Category III AIF has NAV of ₹150 crore. What is the maximum gross exposure it can take under the leverage cap?
₹150 crore
₹300 crore
₹225 crore
₹450 crore
Maximum gross exposure = 2 × NAV = 2 × ₹150 crore = ₹300 crore.
Regulatory Framework
The sponsor or manager of a Category III AIF must maintain a continuing interest of:
The lower of 2.5% of the corpus or ₹5 crore
Exactly 1% of the corpus
Nothing, as Category III is exempt
The lower of 5% of the corpus or ₹10 crore
Category III has a higher skin-in-the-game requirement than Category I and II.
Regulatory Framework
A Category III AIF has a corpus of ₹150 crore. The minimum continuing interest of the sponsor/manager is:
₹7.5 crore
₹10 crore
₹3.75 crore
₹15 crore
5% × ₹150 crore = ₹7.5 crore, which is lower than ₹10 crore.
Regulatory Framework
Which investors are exempt from the ₹1 crore minimum investment requirement in an AIF?
All resident individuals
Any investor introduced by a distributor
Investors in close-ended schemes
Accredited investors
Accredited investors, certified by an accreditation agency, can invest below ₹1 crore.
Regulatory Framework
Individual accredited investor status in India is granted by:
An accreditation agency recognised by SEBI
The AIF's distributor
The investor's bank branch
The fund manager after a phone call
Accreditation agencies (subsidiaries of depositories/exchanges) verify income and net-worth criteria and issue certificates.
Regulatory Framework
From whom should an investor expect to receive the PPM and complete KYC before investing in a Category III AIF?
From the stock exchange website
From the AIF or its manager/distributor, as part of the private placement process
From the RBI
Only after the investment is made
AIF units are privately placed; investors must receive the PPM and complete KYC before subscribing.
Fees Structure, Fund Performance and Benchmarking
A Category III fund's NAV rose from ₹100 to ₹120 in a year. The performance fee is 20% of gains above the high-water mark of ₹100, with no hurdle. Fee per unit is:
Gain above HWM = 120 − 100 = ₹20; 20% × ₹20 = ₹4 per unit.
Fees Structure, Fund Performance and Benchmarking

A fund's NAV starts the year at ₹100 (also the high-water mark), falls to ₹90 at the end of year 1 and rises to ₹110 at the end of year 2. With 20% performance fee on gains above HWM, the year-2 fee per unit is:
Only gains above the HWM of ₹100 earn fees: (110 − 100) × 20% = ₹2; the recovery from 90 to 100 is not charged.
Fees Structure, Fund Performance and Benchmarking
The main purpose of a high-water mark in hedge fund fees is to:
Cap the management fee
Guarantee the investor's capital
Prevent the manager from earning performance fees twice on the same gains after a loss
Set the minimum investment
Performance fees are payable only when NAV exceeds the previous peak on which fees were charged.
Fees Structure, Fund Performance and Benchmarking
A Category III AIF reports a Sharpe ratio. If the fund returned 15%, the risk-free rate was 7% and the fund's standard deviation was 16%, the Sharpe ratio is:
Fees Structure, Fund Performance and Benchmarking
A long-short fund earned 12% while the Nifty 50 TRI earned 18%. The distributor tells a client the fund 'underperformed'. Why is this comparison potentially misleading?
Nifty 50 TRI cannot be used for any fund
Returns of AIFs cannot be compared with anything
A long-short fund has lower net market exposure, so it should be judged against a benchmark reflecting its risk and strategy
Long-short funds are guaranteed to beat indices
Benchmarks should match the strategy's exposure; a long-only index penalises a hedged fund in a rally and flatters it in a fall.
Fees Structure, Fund Performance and Benchmarking
A fund's NAV fell from a peak of ₹150 to a trough of ₹120 before recovering. Its maximum drawdown is:
Maximum drawdown = (150 − 120) / 150 = 20%.
Fees Structure, Fund Performance and Benchmarking
Under SEBI's framework, distribution commission for Category III AIFs must be paid:
Fully upfront
Only on an equal trail basis, with no upfront commission
One-third upfront and the rest on trail
Only from carried interest
Category III AIFs cannot pay upfront distribution commission; it must be on equal trail.
Category III AIF Investment Strategies and Due Diligence Process
A fund buys shares in the cash market and simultaneously sells the same quantity in futures to capture the price difference. This is:
Cash-futures arbitrage
Directional long-only investing
Global macro trading
Venture debt
Buying spot and selling futures locks in the basis, earning a near-risk-free spread if held to expiry.
Category III AIF Investment Strategies and Due Diligence Process
A fund holding long positions of ₹70 crore and short positions of ₹30 crore has a NAV of ₹50 crore. Its gross exposure and net exposure are:
Gross ₹40 crore; net ₹100 crore
Gross ₹100 crore; net ₹40 crore long
Gross ₹70 crore; net ₹30 crore
Gross ₹50 crore; net ₹20 crore
Gross = 70 + 30 = ₹100 crore (2x NAV); net = 70 − 30 = ₹40 crore long.
Category III AIF Investment Strategies and Due Diligence Process
An 'event-driven' strategy seeks to profit from:
Changes in weather
Only the RBI's repo rate decisions
Holding index stocks without trading
Corporate events such as mergers, demergers, buybacks or restructurings
Event-driven managers trade securities whose prices are expected to move due to specific corporate actions.
Category III AIF Investment Strategies and Due Diligence Process
In due diligence of a Category III fund, checking whether the manager's actual trading matches the strategy described in the PPM is a test of:
Survivorship bias
Style drift
Dividend yield
Tax efficiency
Style drift occurs when a manager deviates from the stated strategy, changing the risk the investor signed up for.
Category III AIF Investment Strategies and Due Diligence Process
Which question is most relevant during operational due diligence of a hedge-style AIF?
